history:
The inscription on the lining of this slit tapestry-woven valace...translates as the following: Repair completed at the Yunlin Yuan in the eighth month [August] of the fourth year of [the reign of the] Jiaqing [emperor] [i.e., 1799]. The Yunlin Yuan is probably the name of a Buddhist sub-temple or monastary. Such inscriptions, originally used to keep track to pieces donated to institutions that had large stores of textiles, provide contemporary scholars with important reference points for dating other fabrics of similar style...
Long dragons decorate the main section of this valance. The panel across the top contains a narrative scene of a woman and servant with a barbarian chieftain, probably a reference to the story of Lady Wenji, who was abducted by nomads in the second century B.C. and forced to live on the Central-Asian steppes for twelve years. The reason of this contrast in subject matter is unknown today, but occurs on similar textiles with great regularity.
--John E. Vollmer, Clothed to Rule the Universe: Ming and Qing Dynasty Textiles at the Art Institute of Chicago (2000): 39, plate xxix, cat. 38.
